adversarial.note: every word is a rotation of the same 10-letter multiset, so all n words share one anagram signature (one exact dict key, not merely one hash bucket) and land in a single group; empirically this does NOT degrade to O(n^2) the way distinct-but-colliding keys do, since CPython dicts resolve a repeated exact key by direct slot lookup rather than probing a chain — see README

complexity.notes: word_tuple is computed twice per word (once in the dict comprehension and once in the append loop), doubling the counting work; a single pass with dict.setdefault or collections.defaultdict would be cleaner. The annotation tuple(int) is invalid typing syntax (meant tuple[int, ...]). Since keys are bounded 26-count signatures, hash collisions are bounded, so the worst case does not degrade despite dict usage. With the given scaling (word length bounded independent of n), L is effectively constant, giving linear time overall.
complexity.summary: Each word is mapped to a 26-element character-count tuple, which serves as a hash key to group anagrams in a dictionary; the grouped values are then returned as lists.

complexity.notes: Recursion adds O(log n) call-stack space; an iterative loop would achieve O(1) space. The half-open interval handling with the separate end - start == 1 and == 0 base cases is correct but more verbose than needed; note the recursive helper is defined at module level rather than as a method, which works but is slightly unusual for the NeetCode class-based template.
complexity.summary: Classic recursive binary search: halve the search interval [start, end) each call by comparing the midpoint against the target, with explicit base cases for empty and single-element ranges.

complexity.notes: The half-open interval invariant is handled correctly, including the length-1 case via the final nums[start] check; the final conditional return is slightly convoluted and could be simplified for readability.
complexity.summary: Classic iterative binary search over the sorted array, halving the [start, end) window each iteration and returning the index on equality or -1 after the window collapses.

complexity.notes: best_buy is computed each iteration but never used in the profit calculation (the code uses prices[i] directly), making it dead code; it could have enabled an O(n) solution. Initializing best_buy to 100 also happens to work only because the constraint caps prices at 100.
complexity.summary: Brute-force: for each buy day i, scan all later days j to maximize prices[j] - prices[i], keeping a running best profit floored at 0. Correct but quadratic; a single-pass min-price tracking would give O(n).

complexity.notes: Initializing best_buy to 100 relies on the stated constraint prices[i] <= 100, which is guaranteed, but using float('inf') or prices[0] would be more idiomatic and robust to constraint changes. Iterating directly over values (for price in prices) would also be cleaner than indexing with range(len(prices)).
complexity.summary: Single pass tracking the minimum price seen so far and the maximum profit of selling at each day relative to that minimum. Returns the best profit found, defaulting to 0 if no profitable trade exists.

complexity.notes: The print statement with math.ceil is leftover debugging output that should be removed (it does not affect the result since the actual comparison uses float division, but it wastes I/O time in every iteration). Initializing result = 1 implicitly assumes a non-empty input, which is guaranteed by the stated constraint n >= 1.
complexity.summary: Sorts cars by position descending, then scans from the car nearest the target backward: a car joins the lead fleet if its time to target is at most the lead's, otherwise it starts a new fleet. The sort dominates, giving O(n log n) time.

complexity.notes: The comparison uses float division, which is fine for the stated constraint magnitudes but cross-multiplication would avoid floating-point edge cases; 'import math' is unused; processing via reversed iteration over the sorted list would be more idiomatic than pop().
complexity.summary: Sorts cars by position, then processes from closest to the target backwards, keeping a 'lead' car's arrival time; each car behind either merges into the lead fleet (popped) if it arrives no later, or starts a new fleet. The sort dominates, giving O(n log n) time.

complexity.notes: Works but is unconventional: allocating an O(target) array just to sort by position is wasteful when n << target; sorted(zip(position, speed)) would give O(n) space and O(n log n) time more idiomatically. Correctness relies on positions being unique and below target, both guaranteed by the constraints.
complexity.summary: Places cars into a position-indexed array of size target (which also sorts them by position), then scans from closest-to-target backward, merging any car whose arrival time is no later than the fleet ahead into that fleet and counting a new fleet otherwise.

complexity.notes: The branch guard makes the worst case O(n log n) overall, which is a legitimate optimization, but the magic condition and the 'I asked Claude' comment hurt readability. Arrival times are compared with float division; exact integer cross-multiplication ((target - a.pos) * b.speed vs (target - b.pos) * a.speed) would avoid any floating-point precision concerns.
complexity.summary: Hybrid approach: if target is small relative to n log n, cars are bucketed by position into an array of size target (O(target)); otherwise the cars are sorted by position (O(n log n)). It then scans from the car nearest the destination backward, comparing arrival times to count fleets.

complexity.notes: Storing tuples works, but pushing indices alone and comparing temperatures[stack[-1]] would be cleaner and avoid duplicate storage. The bounded temperature range (1..100) also permits an O(n * 100) next-greater-value alternative, but the stack solution is optimal.
complexity.summary: Monotonic decreasing stack of (temperature, index) pairs; each element is pushed and popped at most once, so when a warmer day arrives it resolves all cooler pending days in amortized O(1) per day.

adversarial.note: n distinct multiples of 2**61-1, all hashing to 0, so every dict insert/lookup collides

complexity.notes: Variable named dict shadows the built-in type. More idiomatic would be a set membership check in a single loop, or simply len(set(nums)) != len(nums); a Counter would also simplify the counting pass.
complexity.summary: Counts occurrences of each value in a hash map over one pass, then makes a second pass to return True as soon as any value has count greater than one. The values come from an input-controlled, unbounded key space, so adversarial hash collisions degrade dict operations to O(n) in the worst case.

complexity.notes: int(a/b) uses float division, which can lose precision for very large intermediate values; a safer truncation is abs(a)//abs(b) with sign handling, though it works within these constraints. Minor: the subtraction trick -pop()+pop() is a bit clever and slightly less readable than explicit a, b pops.
complexity.summary: Evaluates the RPN expression with a stack: pushes parsed operands and, on each operator, pops the top two values, applies the operation, and pushes the result. Division is performed as int(a/b) to truncate toward zero, with operands popped in the correct order.

complexity.notes: Since the alphabet is fixed at 26 lowercase letters, each dict holds at most 26 keys, so lookups are O(1) even adversarially and space is O(1). The manual comparison loops with a bare except are unidiomatic: `multiset_s == multiset_t` (or `collections.Counter(s) == Counter(t)`) does the same job safely and readably; bare `except:` also swallows unrelated errors like KeyboardInterrupt.
complexity.summary: Builds character-frequency dicts for both strings, then compares them by checking that every key in each dict has a matching count in the other, using a bare except to catch missing keys.

complexity.notes: s.lower() creates an O(n) copy; the algorithm itself is in-place otherwise. The inner b-skip loop lacks an explicit bounds check, but it is safe because once a==len(s) the function has already returned True.
complexity.summary: Two-pointer scan from both ends of the lowercased string, skipping non-alphanumeric characters and comparing the rest pairwise. Each pointer moves monotonically, so total work is linear.

complexity.notes: Concise and idiomatic; a two-pointer approach over the original string would reduce space to O(1), but at n <= 1000 the O(n) extra space is immaterial. Note that isalnum() also accepts Unicode alphanumerics beyond ASCII letters/digits, though the constraint of printable ASCII input makes this a non-issue here.
complexity.summary: Filters the lowercased string to alphanumeric characters, builds a cleaned copy, and compares it against its reverse to decide palindrome status.

complexity.notes: Reusing the variable `largest` for both max(heights) and the running best area is confusing; separate variables would be clearer. The standard monotonic-stack solution achieves O(n) without depending on the value bound and is strongly preferred for readability and robustness. The loop `range(largest+1)` also wastes iterations once `largest` has been overwritten by an area value, though this does not affect correctness.
complexity.summary: Brute-force over heights: for each candidate height i from 0 to max(heights), scan all bars to find the longest run of bars with height >= i and track the best area i * run_length. Correct but slow, relying on the bounded value range (heights[i] <= 10,000) to stay feasible.
complexity.time_average: O(n * H) where H = max(heights); since the constraints bound H <= 10^4, this is effectively O(n)
complexity.time_worst: O(n * H) where H = max(heights); with H <= 10^4 guaranteed, O(n)

complexity.notes: Correct only because the problem guarantees length <= 1000; the classic, constraint-free approach is Floyd's tortoise-and-hare in O(n) time and O(1) space. The for/else-free structure is readable, though the magic constant 1005 would be clearer as a named bound.
complexity.summary: Exploits the stated length cap (<= 1000): it follows next pointers at most 1005 times; if null is reached the list terminates (no cycle), otherwise the list must contain a cycle.

adversarial.note: n distinct multiples of 2**61-1, all hashing to 0, so every set insert/lookup collides

complexity.notes: Per the scaling note values are a permutation of range(n), so integer keys hash without adversarial collisions and lookups remain O(1) worst case. The pop-and-expand style is slightly less readable than the canonical 'only start from run beginnings' loop, but the destructive removal guarantees linear total work.
complexity.summary: Builds a set, then repeatedly pops an arbitrary element and expands outward in both directions to extract its entire consecutive run, removing each element as it is consumed so every element is processed exactly once.

complexity.notes: Correct but slightly convoluted head-selection logic; a dummy head node would make the code cleaner and avoid the duplicated return statements. Strictly speaking it mutates/reuses the input nodes rather than building new ones, which the problem explicitly allows.
complexity.summary: Iteratively merges the two sorted lists with two pointers, splicing existing nodes onto a merged chain rooted at the smaller head, then appends the non-empty remainder in O(1).

complexity.notes: Initializing min_stack with float('inf') is a clean sentinel that avoids empty-checks in push. Space is O(n) in the worst case (monotonically decreasing pushes), which is inherent to this design.
complexity.summary: Auxiliary min-stack approach: a second stack stores running minima, pushing a value only when it is <= the current minimum and popping it when the popped main value equals the current minimum. All four operations are O(1) list-index operations, so a sequence of n calls costs O(n) total.

complexity.notes: Uses the division approach, so it does not meet the follow-up requirement (prefix/suffix products without division would be preferred). The slices nums[:zero] and nums[zero+1:] allocate extra O(n) memory; indexing directly would avoid that. Also, 'case x if x > 1' works but 'case _' after checking 'a > 1' first would be clearer.
complexity.summary: Counts zeros with a match statement: with 2+ zeros all outputs are 0, with 1 zero only that position gets the product of the rest, otherwise divides the total product by each element.

complexity.notes: Correct but slightly awkward structure: the loop condition handles the tail node's relinking after the loop, whereas the standard idiom (while curr: save next, flip, advance) handles everything inside the loop and also subsumes the head-is-None/single-node edge cases.
complexity.summary: Iteratively reverses the singly linked list in a single pass by redirecting each node's next pointer to its predecessor, tracking previous/current/next nodes.

complexity.notes: Correct but unnecessarily allocates O(n) auxiliary storage; the standard iterative three-pointer reversal achieves O(1) space. Note that for i=0, nodes[i-1] is nodes[-1] (the None sentinel), which works but is a subtle negative-indexing trick that may hurt readability.
complexity.summary: Collects all nodes into a Python list (including a trailing None sentinel), then rewires each node's next pointer to its predecessor by iterating the list, and returns the former tail as the new head.

complexity.notes: Correct under the problem's stated ASCII-only constraint, since the emoji delimiter cannot appear in the input; however, this fails the follow-up requirement of handling any possible character set, where a length-prefixed encoding would be needed. The empty-list special case is a minor wart (decode('') returns [] only because of the trailing pop).
complexity.summary: Encode joins all strings with an emoji delimiter (plus a trailing delimiter), and decode splits on that delimiter and drops the empty trailing element.

complexity.notes: Correctness flaw: the problem guarantees strs[i] may contain ANY of 256 ASCII characters, so an input string can contain the delimiter itself (e.g. ['paysutdlfmywvaugplk49w87ky9v478']), making decode return extra/wrong segments. A length-prefixed encoding (e.g. 'len#string') is the correct approach. Edge cases like [] and [''] happen to work, but the delimiter collision violates the stated constraints.
complexity.summary: Encodes by joining the strings with a fixed 'random-looking' delimiter (plus a trailing delimiter), and decodes by splitting on that delimiter and dropping the empty trailing piece. Both passes are a single linear scan over the total character volume, which scales linearly with n.

complexity.notes: decode is quadratic because s = s[a+1+...:] copies the rest of the string every iteration; using an index pointer (or iter over a single pass) instead of re-slicing would make it O(n). s.index('|') is fine here since the delimiter always appears within the short numeric prefix at the current position.
complexity.summary: Encodes each string as a length-prefix plus the string itself (O(n) total via join). Decode repeatedly parses the prefix and re-slices the remainder of the input; since each slice copies the remaining O(n) characters, decoding is O(n^2) overall.

adversarial.note: n distinct multiples of 2**61-1, all hashing to 0, so every dict insert/lookup collides

complexity.notes: Keys are drawn from the bounded range [-1000, 1000] per the constraints, so hash collisions are bounded and dict lookups remain O(1) worst case. The counting loop does a redundant double lookup ('num in num_counts' then num_counts[num]); dict.get(num, 0) or collections.Counter would be cleaner. The final set() dedup can silently return more or fewer than k elements when frequencies tie, which works here only because the answer is guaranteed unique; a heapq.nlargest over items would be O(n + d log k) and more direct.
complexity.summary: Counts frequencies in a dict, sorts the distinct frequency values and takes the top k, then collects all keys matching those frequencies and deduplicates with a set. Sorting the up-to-n distinct counts dominates the runtime.

adversarial.note: n distinct multiples of 2**61-1, all hashing to 0, so every dict insert/lookup collides

complexity.notes: The nums.index() calls are O(n) linear scans each (still dominated by the sort), and nums.pop() mutates the caller's input list, which is poor practice. A dict-based single pass would achieve O(n) average time and avoid the index-recovery awkwardness.
complexity.summary: Sorts a copy of the array and uses a two-pointer scan to find the pair summing to target, then recovers the original indices via linear nums.index() searches, with special handling when the pair is a duplicated value.

adversarial.note: n distinct multiples of 2**61-1 (already ascending), all hashing to 0, so every dict insert/lookup collides

complexity.notes: Sorting is unnecessary since the input is guaranteed pre-sorted, and the nums2 copy plus the O(1)-space requirement in the problem statement are violated (uses O(n) extra space). The index() calls are O(n) each but remain dominated by the O(n log n) sort; correctness is fine given the exactly-one-solution guarantee.
complexity.summary: Sorts a copy of the array, then runs a two-pointer scan from both ends to find the pair summing to target, and finally recovers the original 1-indexed positions via linear index() lookups (with a pop to disambiguate duplicate values).

complexity.notes: Using list.count inside a loop makes each line check O(k^2) in the line length k, which is fine here (k=9) but a set-based check would be the idiomatic O(k) pattern. Multiplying booleans with 'valid *=' works but 'valid = valid and ...' or all() would be clearer; also List is used without an import.
complexity.summary: Validates each row, column, and 3x3 box by checking that no non-empty cell's digit appears more than once in that line, using list.count for the duplicate check. Since the board is always 9x9, all 27 line validations run in constant time.

complexity.notes: The pop() calls rely on short-circuit evaluation (pop only executes when the bracket matches the elif condition), which is correct but slightly subtle to read. A dict mapping closing to opening brackets would be more idiomatic and avoid the repeated elif chain; membership testing against the 3-element list is fine but a set or tuple literal would be more conventional.
complexity.summary: Classic stack-based validation: push each opening bracket, and on each closing bracket pop and verify the types match; the string is valid iff the stack is empty at the end. Uses a constant-size list membership test instead of a hash map, so no hashing is involved.

complexity.notes: Clean and idiomatic; the fixed literal mapping keeps both correctness and constant-time lookups independent of hash randomness.
complexity.summary: Classic stack-based validation: push opening brackets, and on each closing bracket pop and check it matches via a fixed close-to-open mapping; the string is valid iff the stack ends empty. The dict keys come from a constant 6-character alphabet, so lookups are O(1) even in the worst case.
